This yields matrix Grassmannian primitives and tensor Grassmannian primitives that are compact, data-adaptive, and directly decodable by explicit multilinear reconstruction. Theoretically, we prove that the proposed primitive maps are homeomorphisms between low-rank tensors and their corresponding primitive spaces, certifying that the representations are non-degenerate and topologically faithful. Building on these primitives, we propose *Diffusion in Aligned Tensor Space* (DiffATS), a generative framework that trains diffusion models directly on aligned tensor primitives. Across images, videos, and PDE solutions, DiffATS achieves strong unconditional and conditional generation performance while compressing original data by $3.9\times$ to $210\times$, without relying on any pretrained deep compression autoencoders.
  </details>

- **[iMuon: Intrinsic Spectral Optimization on Riemannian Matrix Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09238)**  `arXiv:2605.09238`  
  _Yibang Li, Bihari Lal Pandey, Ravi Sah, Andi Han, Cyrus Mostajeran, Pratik Jawanpuria, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Muon and related norm-constrained optimizers, now central to large-scale learning, compute updates via a linear maximization oracle (LMO) over a matrix-norm ball in Euclidean space. However, they do not generalize cleanly to manifold-valued parameters such as low-rank factorizations, orthogonality constraints, or symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrices. Naively restricting the Muon LMO to the tangent space (i) breaks quotient symmetries and (ii) couples the tangent-space constraint with an ambient norm bound, which obstructs closed-form solutions. We resolve both issues with a key observation: every Riemannian metric canonically lifts a unitarily invariant Euclidean norm to an intrinsic norm on each tangent space. The resulting intrinsic LMO is symmetry preserving and, under a structural condition on the scaled tangent space, reduces to a standard Euclidean LMO. Building on this, we introduce intrinsic Muon (iMuon), a unified framework with closed-form updates on the fixed-rank, SPD, Stiefel, and Grassmann manifolds for various unitarily invariant norms, including the spectral, Frobenius, and nuclear norms. We establish deterministic and stochastic convergence rates of iMuon with constants that depend only on the manifold dimension. Notably, on the fixed-rank manifold, the constant depends only on the rank, which makes the rate independent of factor conditioning and removes the runtime factor rescaling required by prior work. Experiments on LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs, image classification, and subspace learning illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.
  </details>

- **[Transferable SCF-Acceleration through Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21657)**  `arXiv:2604.21657`  
  _Eike S. Eberhard, Viktor Kotsev, Timm Güthle, Stephan Günnemann_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The cost of Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) calculations scales with the number of required solver iterations, which depend on the quality of the initial guess. Machine learning methods that predict initial guesses from molecular geometry can reduce this cost, but matrix-prediction models fail when extrapolating to larger molecules, degrading rather than accelerating convergence [Liu et al., 2025]. We show that this failure is a supervision problem, not an extrapolation problem: models trained on ground-state targets fit those targets well out of distribution, yet produce initial guesses that slow convergence. Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning (SAIL) resolves this for both Hamiltonian and density matrix models by differentiating through parts of the self-consistent field (SCF) solver end-to-end. We introduce the Effective Relative Iteration Count (ERIC), a correction to the commonly used RIC that accounts for hidden Fock-build overhead. On QM40, which contains molecules up to 4$\times$ larger than the training distribution, SAIL reduces ERIC by 40% (PBE), 35% (SCAN), and 32% (B3LYP), more than doubling the previous state-of-the-art reduction on B3LYP. On QMugs molecules 10$\times$ larger than the training set, SAIL delivers a 1.35$\times$ wall-time speedup at the hybrid level of theory, extending ML SCF acceleration to large drug-like molecules.
  </details>

- **[Differentially Private Non-convex Distributionally Robust Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16155)**  `arXiv:2602.16155`  
  _Difei Xu, Meng Ding, Zebin Ma, Huanyi Xie, Youming Tao, Aicha Slaitane, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Real-world deployments routinely face distribution shifts, group imbalances, and adversarial perturbations, under which the traditional Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) framework can degrade severely.Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses this issue by optimizing the worst-case expected loss over an uncertainty set of distributions, offering a principled approach to robustness.Meanwhile, as training data in DRO always involves sensitive information, safeguarding it against leakage under Differential Privacy (DP) is essential.In contrast to classical DP-ERM, DP-DRO has received much less attention due to its minimax optimization structure with uncertainty constraint.To bridge the gap, we provide a comprehensive study of DP-(finite-sum)-DRO with $\psi$-divergence and non-convex loss.First, we study DRO with general $\psi$-divergence by reformulating it as a minimization problem, and develop a novel $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP optimization method, called DP Double-Spider, tailored to this structure.Under mild assumptions, we show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+ (\frac{\sqrt{d \log (1/\delta)}}{n \varepsilon})^{2/3})$ in terms of the gradient norm, where $n$ denotes the data size and $d$ denotes the model dimension.We further improve the utility rate for specific divergences.In particular, for DP-DRO with KL-divergence, by transforming the problem into a compositional finite-sum optimization problem, we develop a DP Recursive-Spider method and show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d \log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3} )$, matching the best-known result for non-convex DP-ERM.Experimentally, we demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing approaches for DP minimax optimization.
  </details>

- **[GPTZero: Robust Detection of LLM-Generated Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13042)**  `arXiv:2602.13042`  
  _George Alexandru Adam, Alexander Cui, Edwin Thomas, Emily Napier, Nazar Shmatko, Yue Gao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While historical considerations surrounding text authenticity revolved primarily around plagiarism, the advent of large language models (LLMs) has introduced a new challenge: distinguishing human-authored from AI-generated text. This shift raises significant concerns, including the undermining of skill evaluations, the mass-production of low-quality content, and the proliferation of misinformation. Addressing these issues, we introduce GPTZero 5.0, a state-of-the-art industrial AI detection solution, offering reliable discernment between human and LLM-generated text. Our key contributions include: introducing a hierarchical, multi-task architecture enabling a flexible taxonomy of human and AI texts, setting a new state-of-the-art for AI detection accuracy on 11 independent third-party benchmarks and 18 writing domains, and achieving superior robustness to adversarial attacks and paraphrasing via multi-tiered automated red teaming. GPTZero offers accurate and explainable detection, and educates users on its responsible use, ensuring fair and transparent assessment of text.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Success Rates: Trainability and Extractability for Offline GCRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05459)**  `arXiv:2602.05459`  
  _Jan Malte Töpperwien, Aditya Mohan, Marius Lindauer_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) methods are typically benchmarked by the success rates of optimized hyperparameter configurations. However, success rate by itself does not provide information about the sensitivity of algorithms to hyperparameters for value learning or policy extraction, since an algorithm could obtain the same success rate across a wide range of hyperparameters, or might succeed only on specific settings. We study this phenomenon in the offline GCRL algorithms GCIQL, GCIVL, QRL, and CRL under a shared policy extractor, by constructing landscapes of interaction between the learning rate and policy extraction hyperparameters such as the temperature of advantage-weighted regression (AWR). These landscapes reveal large, task-dependent differences in hyperparameter sensitivity. On AntMaze-M, 59% of QRL configurations and 66% of CRL configurations achieve at least 90% of the method's best sampled success rate, compared with 3% for both GCIQL and GCIVL. On Cube and Scene, GCIQL and GCIVL instead attain higher success over broader hyperparameter regions than QRL and CRL. To interpret these differences, we analyze how reliably learned advantages rank actual goals from the same trajectory above random goals, and how strongly AWR concentrates policy updates on a small subset of transitions. Our findings indicate strongly differing behavior of these algorithms at policy-extraction time, even under the same success rates. Given these results, we argue that offline GCRL methods should be evaluated by both attainable success and the needed hyperparameter range to sustain it, complemented by post-hoc diagnostics to understand the signal used to train the policy. The overview and code are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Agentic AI-Empowered Dynamic Survey Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04071)**  `arXiv:2602.04071`  
  _Furkan Mumcu, Lokman Bekit, Michael J. Jones, Anoop Cherian, Yasin Yilmaz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Survey papers play a central role in synthesizing and organizing scientific knowledge, yet they are increasingly strained by the rapid growth of research output. As new work continues to appear after publication, surveys quickly become outdated, contributing to redundancy and fragmentation in the literature. We reframe survey writing as a long-horizon maintenance problem rather than a one-time generation task, treating surveys as living documents that evolve alongside the research they describe. We propose an agentic Dynamic Survey Framework that supports the continuous updating of existing survey papers by incrementally integrating new work while preserving survey structure and minimizing unnecessary disruption. Using a retrospective experimental setup, we demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively identifies and incorporates emerging research while preserving the coherence and structure of existing surveys, even over extended sequences of updates.
  </details>

- **[Cross-Epoch Bias in SGD-based Leave-One-Out Influence: Analysis and Accumulative Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26185)**  `arXiv:2510.26185`  
  _Yunxiao Shi, Shuo Yang, Yixin Su, Rui Zhang, Min Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Training-data influence estimates support data selection and cleansing by predicting the effects of removing individual examples. The standard multi-epoch SGD-Influence Estimator (SGD-IE) aggregates contributions from a sample's repeated appearances along the recorded trajectory. When used to approximate finite deletion, it omits an interaction: later removals act on the parameter displacement accumulated from earlier removals. We introduce the Accumulative SGD-Influence Estimator (ACC-SGD-IE) to account for how earlier removals change the effect of removing the same sample again. It uses the sample's Hessian at subsequent appearances to correct the estimated parameter change. Our non-convex analysis shows that this correction removes SGD-IE's additional interaction contribution from the finite-horizon error bound: the omitted interaction produces a local error linear in the accumulated parameter change, while the remaining Taylor remainder is bounded quadratically under Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions. The bounds characterize how training propagates the remaining error. In non-convex experiments across clean and noisy tabular, text, and vision datasets, ACC-SGD-IE reduces validation-loss-change RMSE by 10.8% and improves Jaccard@10% by 15.2% on average relative to SGD-IE. These gains also translate into lower test misclassification rates after data cleansing on MNIST and CIFAR10 at the evaluated removal budgets. On noisy industrial datasets, it reduces aggregate parameter RMS error with a mean relative reduction of 53.4%. We further discuss computational tradeoffs, provide complementary theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation for strongly convex objectives, and explore potential extensions of the accumulative correction mechanism to other influence estimators.
  </details>

- **[Interpret Policies in Deep Reinforcement Learning using SILVER with RL-Guided Labeling: A Model-level Approach to High-dimensional and Multi-action Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19244)**  `arXiv:2510.19244`  
  _Yiyu Qian, Liyuan Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep reinforcement learning (RL) achieves remarkable performance but lacks interpretability, limiting trust in policy behavior. The existing SILVER framework (Li, Siddique, and Cao 2025) explains RL policy via Shapley-based regression but remains restricted to low-dimensional, binary-action domains. We propose SILVER with RL-guided labeling, an enhanced variant that extends SILVER to multi-action and high-dimensional environments by incorporating the RL policy's own action outputs into the boundary points identification. Our method first extracts compact feature representations from image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution, and then employs RL-guided labeling to generate behaviorally consistent boundary datasets. Surrogate models, such as decision trees and regression-based functions, are subsequently trained to interpret RL policy's decision structure. We evaluate the proposed framework on two Atari environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the derived interpretable policy. Results show that our approach maintains competitive task performance while substantially improving transparency and human understanding of agent behavior. This work advances explainable RL by transforming SILVER into a scalable and behavior-aware framework for interpreting deep RL agents in high-dimensional, multi-action settings.
  </details>

- **[Learning Greens Operators through Hierarchical Neural Networks Inspired by the Fast Multipole Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20591)**  `arXiv:2509.20591`  
  _Emilio McAllister Fognini, Marta M. Betcke, Ben T. Cox_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an efficient numerical algorithm for computation of long-ranged forces in $N$-body problems within gravitational and electrostatic fields. This method utilizes multipole expansions of the Green's function inherent to the underlying dynamical systems. Despite its widespread application in physics and engineering, the integration of FMM with modern machine learning architectures remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a novel neural network architecture, the Neural FMM, that integrates the information flow of the FMM into a hierarchical machine learning framework for learning the Green's operator of an Elliptic PDE. Our Neural FMM architecture leverages a hierarchical computation flow of the FMM method to split up the local and far-field interactions and efficiently learn their respective representations.
  </details>

- **[Recursive Learning-Based Virtual Buffering for Analytical Global Placement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17247)**  `arXiv:2506.17247`  
  _Andrew B. Kahng, Yiting Liu, Zhiang Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Due to the skewed scaling of interconnect versus cell delay in modern technology nodes, placement with buffer porosity (i.e., cell density) awareness is essential for timing closure in physical synthesis flows. However, existing approaches face two key challenges: (i) traditional van Ginneken-Lillis-style buffering approaches are computationally expensive during global placement; and (ii) machine learning-based approaches, such as BufFormer, lack a thorough consideration of Electrical Rule Check (ERC) violations and fail to "close the loop" back into the physical design flow. In this work, we propose MLBuf-RePlAce, the first open-source learning-driven virtual buffering-aware analytical global placement framework, built on top of the OpenROAD infrastructure. MLBuf-RePlAce adopts an efficient recursive learning-based generative buffering approach to predict buffer types and locations, addressing ERC violations during global placement. We compare MLBuf-RePlAce against the default virtual buffering-based timing-driven global placer in OpenROAD, using open-source testcases from the TILOS MacroPlacement and OpenROAD-flow-scripts repositories. Without degradation of post-route power, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (56%, 31%) in total negative slack (TNS) within the open-source OpenROAD flow. When evaluated by completion in a commercial flow, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (53%, 28%) in TNS with an average of 0.2% improvement in post-route power.
  </details>

- **[HOPSE: Scalable Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder for Combinatorial Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15405)**  `arXiv:2505.15405`  
  _Guillermo Bernárdez, Marco Montagna, Louis Van Langendonck, Martin Carrasco, Amirreza Akbari, Louisa Cornelis, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective at modeling relational data, pairwise connections cannot fully capture multi-way relationships naturally present in complex real-world systems. In response to this, Topological Deep Learning (TDL) leverages more general combinatorial representations--such as simplicial or cellular complexes--to accommodate higher-order interactions. Existing TDL methods often extend GNNs through Higher-Order Message Passing (HOMP), but face critical scalability challenges due to the steep complexity overhead of propagating messages through combinatorial structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose HOPSE (Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder), a framework free of learnable message passing layers that uses Hasse graph decompositions to derive efficient and expressive encodings over arbitrary higher-order domains. Notably, HOPSE training and inference scale linearly with the size of combinatorial representations while preserving the expressive power and permutation equivariance of the HOMP approaches. Experiments on molecular and topological benchmarks show that it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance while consistently achieving speedups over HOMP-based models, opening a new path for scalable TDL. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[SiGMA: Learning under Graph-Level Heterogeneity with Gated Message-Passing and Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00547)**  `arXiv:2503.00547`  
  _Raphael Pellegrin, Lukas Fesser, Melanie Weber_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In graph-level learning, graph neural networks are typically applied with a fixed computational template: the same depth, local message-passing operator, and global attention mechanism are used for every input graph. However, different graphs within the same dataset can vary substantially in prediction difficulty and may require different mixtures of local and non-local computation. We study this phenomenon as graph-level heterogeneity in both classification and regression tasks. To address it, we propose SiGMA (Sigmoid Gated Message-Passing and Attention), a gated hybrid graph neural network architecture that combines message-passing and attention heads within each layer. Inspired by the growing use of gated attention and gated computation in large language models and vision transformers, each head in SiGMA is modulated by a learned node-wise sigmoid gate, allowing the model to adaptively regulate which local or global mechanisms are active for different nodes, layers, and input graphs. The resulting architecture can emulate expressive message-passing backbones, admits near-identity computation paths that are not forced to over-smooth, and enables direct non-local communication beyond message-passing neighborhoods to mitigate over-squashing. Empirically, SiGMA achieves strong performance across graph-level benchmarks, consistently matching or improving over competitive graph transformer and hybrid baselines. Our results suggest that adapting computation to graph-level heterogeneity is a promising direction for building more flexible and effective graph learning architectures.
  </details>

- **[Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22632)**  `arXiv:2611.22632`  
  _Takahiro Ezaki, Naoto Imura, Katsuhiro Nishinari_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all five models tested left capacity unused. Keeping the success record fixed, we gave agents numbers without instructions, using each value equally often but giving group members either identical or distinct numbers. With OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol or Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, distinct numbers spread simultaneous requests across servers and increased job completions even though overall choice frequencies barely changed. Telling AI agents which resources are available leaves a second design challenge: helping them spread demand across those resources.
  </details>

- **[Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22461)**  `arXiv:2611.22461`  
  _Ziaullah Khan, Abdul Rehman Khalid, Shrestha Nischal Lal, Nheng Vanchhay, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Hee-Cheol Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.
  </details>

- **[Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22067)**  `arXiv:2611.22067`  
  _Seongmin Kim, Woohyeon Byeon, Jiwon Jeon, Seungyul Han, Youngchul Sung_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.
  </details>

- **[Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21828)**  `arXiv:2611.21828`  
  _Jongann Lee, Melkior Ornik_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.
  </details>

- **[Even Loose Proximity Constraints Make Makespan-optimal Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding Hard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21277)**  `arXiv:2611.21277`  
  _Takahiro Suzuki, Keisuke Okumura_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study $r$-Connected Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding ($r$CUMAPF), a variant of MAPF where interchangeable agents have a proximity range $r\in \mathbb{N}$, and agents must form a single group in a given graph $G$ through limited-range communication at all times. The problem arises in fundamental applications such as self-reconfiguration and platooning, while standard MAPF does not capture proximity constraints. For the problem of finding a makespan-optimal solution, prior work shows NP-hardness for $r=1$ and polynomial-time solvability when $r$ is sufficiently large; the complexity for the intermediate case $2\le r$ is largely unknown. To narrow this gap, we show that finding a solution to $r$CUMAPF with makespan at most $2$ is NP-hard for $2\le r= O(|V|^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $0<\varepsilon\le 1$ is a fixed constant and $|V|$ is the number of vertices. As a consequence, we show that the labeled analogue of $r$CUMAPF is also NP-hard under the same condition.
  </details>

- **[Equilibrium decisions under partial observation: dynamical error bounds and information requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14815)**  `arXiv:2607.14815`  
  _Ali Ghoroghi, Yacine Rezgui, Afrouz Ghaemi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reduced monitoring can preserve stable dynamics while changing an equilibrium decision. Motivated by heterogeneous urban-mobility indicator coverage, we study fixed linear observations of a nonlinear recovery flow coupled to a strategic fixed-point map, and ask when a decision based on the reduced model can be trusted. The main result is a joint certificate: bounds on trajectory tracking, equilibrium displacement and unresolved output dependence are assembled into one decision-margin error which, under a stated Gaussian observation model, yields a conservative one-sided test and an explicit information requirement for prescribed worst-case power. In the scalar experiment this requirement is sharp: when the effect does not exceed twice the error budget, no valid test has worst-case power above its size, however many observations are taken. A second result connects manifold-adapted observations to defect bounds through a locally invertible observation chart, while distinguishing observation initialisation from asymptotic phase initialisation. Supporting results, resting on established lumping, contraction and fixed-point theory, cover exact quotients, an observation-fibre obstruction and the dependence of recovery-time comparisons on the tolerance convention. Seven reproducible synthetic experiments examine each component. The results give conditional criteria for certifying partial monitoring and separate mathematical guarantees from empirical validation.
  </details>

- **[TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23143)**  `arXiv:2611.23143`  
  _Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
  </details>

- **[Pressure Drop: Gravity Vector Estimation from a Distributed Barometric Pressure Sensor Array](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23120)**  `arXiv:2611.23120`  
  _William Dubois, Nicolas Lauzon, Johann Laconte, François Pomerleau_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While gravity is often used in mobile robotics as a global constraint for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms, most estimation methods rely on indirect observation of the gravity vector. In this paper, we propose the use of altimeter measurements to directly observe the direction of the gravity vector. We provide a theoretical evaluation of the estimation noise and validate it through extensive experimental data, along with an evaluation of the impact of intersensor distance on our gravity vector estimates. Experimental results demonstrate that a median error of $0.87^\circ$ on the tilt estimation can be achieved with our system in semi-static scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this approach by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods based on Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs). We highlight that we achieve similar performance to that of IMU-based systems in highly dynamic scenarios and even outperform in specific cases of accelerometer measurement saturation. Finally, an additional experiment shows the potential use within a robotic system through the integration into an Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm.
  </details>

- **[Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23118)**  `arXiv:2611.23118`  
  _Joyjeet Singh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.
  </details>

- **[CADENCE: Learning Acyclic Gaits for Model-Based Quadruped Locomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23102)**  `arXiv:2611.23102`  
  _Owen Sullivan, Sourav Selvaraj, Mahdi Agheli_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model-based quadruped controllers usually step on a cyclic gait, which lifts the legs in a fixed order on a fixed period, wherever the safe footholds are. We present CADENCE, a learned step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it picks one of at most 65 discrete choices: no step, or one leg's step to a safe foothold. It also predicts a swing time. We train CADENCE by reinforcement learning on top of a convex model predictive controller (MPC). Nothing prescribes a gait: there is no gait schedule, and the reward has no gait term, only a cost per step. The one structural constraint is that at most two legs may swing at once. The policy we analyzed developed an acyclic gait, with no fixed period or stepping order, yet it still paired diagonal legs. An inverse footstep model (IFM), fitted on a controller's logged steps, turns each foothold into a command. With only the IFM refitted, on fewer than 20,000 steps, CADENCE ran frozen on OCS2's nonlinear MPC. In simulated trials on a range of terrains (26% to 49% voids) and speeds (0.1 m/s and 0.2 m/s), it succeeded in 85.1% (mean of five seeds), against 67.8% for OCS2-Trot, 65.5% for OCS2-Single, and 39.6% in a static walk ablation of CADENCE. At 49% voids, it succeeded in 72.9%, against 43.0% for OCS2-Trot.
  </details>

- **[PAIR: Bringing Household Robots into the Smart Home](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23070)**  `arXiv:2611.23070`  
  _Junseong Pyo, Hyeongjin Kim, Jongwook Han, Seungwon Kook, Sungjib Lim, Yohan Jo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{this https URL}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}
  </details>

- **[RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23056)**  `arXiv:2611.23056`  
  _Jiarui Guo, Saining Zhang, Jiaying Wan, Jiawei Weng, Junhao Chen, Rui Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.
  </details>

- **[Making Future-Predictive Representations Actionable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22994)**  `arXiv:2611.22994`  
  _Fangchuan Wang, Hao Zhang, Qiyan Zhao, Huanqi Zhao, Guanting Ye, Xu-Yao Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.
  </details>

- **[Physics-Informed Tactile-based Shape Estimation of Deformable Linear Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22990)**  `arXiv:2611.22990`  
  _Rotem Atari, Stav Ashur, Avishai Sintov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Accurate shape estimation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation, often hindered by visual occlusions and the high-dimensional configuration space of flexible materials. While Force/Torque (F/T) and vision-centric methods have been proposed, they frequently struggle with grasp-site ambiguities and environmental interference. In this letter, we investigate the hypothesis that global shape estimation can be achieved through tactile sensing and proprioception, without any visual perception. We contend that dense, high-resolution tactile imprints capture critical boundary conditions and contact gradients that are sufficient to resolve the high-dimensional configuration of the DLO. To prove this, we introduce a Physics-Informed Vision Transformer (ViT) framework that maps tactile images to a 3D vertex chain. By leveraging self-attention mechanisms and a physics-weighted loss function, our model enforces structural priors to ensure that the predicted geometry adheres to the object's physical manifold. Experimental results demonstrate that our tactile-based approach achieves superior reconstruction accuracy across Euclidean and Chamfer metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficiency of this modality, achieving model transfer to novel DLO materials and geometries. Our findings suggest that tactile feedback provides a robust and computationally efficient alternative for DLO state estimation in visually degraded or occluded environments.
  </details>

- **[Sideslip-Conditioned Drift Trajectory Planning with Flow Matching and Control Barrier Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22927)**  `arXiv:2611.22927`  
  _Seokjun Lee, Seung-Hyun Kong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Drifting, the deliberate control of a vehicle at large sideslip angles, is relevant to both motorsport and recovery from unexpected oversteer. Existing autonomous drifting methods typically determine drift intensity through predefined reference trajectories, optimization objectives, or learned policy rewards, rather than accepting a desired sideslip angle as an explicit input. We propose, to the best of our knowledge, the first generative drift trajectory planner explicitly conditioned on a requested peak sideslip angle.
