A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.
  </details>

- **[Future Prediction as Training-Only Video Supervision for Pretrained VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34593)**  `arXiv:2610.34593`

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire rich visual and semantic representations as well as action-generation capabilities. Their action objectives typically lack direct supervision for predicting future visual observations. Future videos in robot demonstrations record object motion and task progress. They can provide temporal visual supervision that complements action labels.We propose Training-Only Video Supervision, which introduces future-video prediction as an auxiliary objective for VLA fine-tuning. We condition a randomly initialized video-prediction expert on the VLA's shared vision-language features. The expert learns to predict future video latents from robot demonstrations. The video prediction loss and the original action loss jointly update the shared vision-language backbone, providing additional temporal visual supervision. After training, we remove the video expert and its adapter. The fine-tuned VLA retains its original action-generation pathway at inference. On the 50-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, our method achieves 71.18% average success, compared with $\pi_{0.5}$ of 58.33%. In a matched evaluation on four real-world manipulation tasks, success increases from 42.50% to 61.25%. These results show that future visual modeling can serve as auxiliary training supervision for pretrained VLAs. The fine-tuned action policy benefits from this supervision without retaining a video-prediction branch at deployment.
  </details>

- **[On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27275)**  `arXiv:2610.27275`  
  _Abolfazl Babanazari, Kaveh Fathian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically. We show that, at any fixed positive tolerance, a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. We also study group-$k$ consistency, which uses consistency of groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge2$. Finally, our experiments on nearly 8,000 registration examples quantify the frequency of these limitations in practice and show how the derived bounds can be used to check whether a subset of matches can be aligned within a point tolerance.
  </details>

- **[Foundation-Model-Driven 3D Scene Graphs for Mobile Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23622)**  `arXiv:2610.23622`  
  _Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
  </details>

- **[Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18352)**  `arXiv:2610.18352`  
  _Youpeng Wen, Gang Wang, Tianyu Huang, Weiwei Zhang, Zhijian Huang, Wei Chen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects.Our code and project page are available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Stereo-Planner: Learning Stereo-to-Trajectory Planning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Quadrotor Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15560)**  `arXiv:2610.15560`  
  _Hongming Shen, Junjie Lu, Xun Chen, Wei Wang, Xinhang Xu, Bailing Tian, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of approaching 8 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 14.44 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[No Need to Stop the Fleet: Localized Anomaly Isolation via Dead Zones in AGV Fleets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08524)**  `arXiv:2610.08524`  
  _Natalia Ogorelysheva, Falk Howar, Jian-Jia Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) fleets in production and logistics environments rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies such as malfunctions, hazards, or contaminated areas. While safe, this approach halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. This paper proposes dead zones -- a formally defined localized isolation approach that serves as an additional fail-operational mechanism for situations where a full system-wide halt is not strictly needed. Rather than shutting down the entire fleet, a dead zone isolates the anomalous area, allowing unaffected robots to continue operating normally. We introduce two operational strategies: basic dead zone handling, in which affected robots enter a dead zone and stop, and dead zone handling with escaping, in which robots that are sufficiently far from a dead zone reroute around it. For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories we prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation is kept between robots. Experimental evaluation confirms the theoretical guarantees and characterizes the throughput tradeoffs between all three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.
  </details>

- **[DASH: A da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid Robots as an Accessible Platform for Surgical Robotics Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05792)**  `arXiv:2610.05792`  
  _Sara Wickenhiser, Junrong Zhou, Zekai Liang, Lizzie Peiros, Liu Shanglei, Michael C. Yip_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robotic minimally invasive surgery offers well-documented clinical benefits, but the cost and infrastructure requirements of purpose-built platforms limit access in rural and lower-resourced facilities. Recent work has teleoperated general-purpose robots for laparoscopic tasks and in vivo procedures, but relied on handheld instruments coupled through passive linkages rather than native robotic actuation. Instead, we adapt da Vinci Classic and Xi instruments onto general-purpose robots that can integrate in clinical workflows. We present DASH, a da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid platforms, consisting of two types of adapters that require no modification to the instruments themselves. Each adapter is compatible with many robotic platform load capacities, engages the instrument's native latch, and wirelessly identifies inserted tools to load instrument-specific kinematics and coupling matrices. Teleoperated experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DASH and its benefits for enabling research access to surgical robotic platforms. DASH has been open sourced atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[AVL-JEPA: Preventing Causal Dynamics Information Collapse In Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03587)**  `arXiv:2610.03587`  
  _Yikang Qiao, Ling Zhang, Ziying Song, Duan Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict future latent representations without reconstructing observations, enabling world models to focus on high-level semantic dynamics. However, a JEPA can preserve high dimensional visual information while discarding information about the physical consequences of actions. We call this failure mode causal dynamics information collapse and propose action-grounded vision-invariance latent (AVL) to prevent this collapse. We first use the executed action as an auxiliary dynamics anchor that encourages the model to preserve dynamics information, and then use a vision-invariance pathway which aligns perturbed and clean latent predictions without discarding dynamics information, forcing the model to fully understand and utilize causal dynamics information. We validate AVL on four robotic control tasks (TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench Cube, and Reacher), showing that it substantially improves success rates under visual perturbations while preserving clean-environment performance. We further evaluate physical consequence alignment, clean-noisy dynamics consistency, and the causal effect of targeted transition subspace erasure. Collectively, these results indicate that dynamic information causally relevant to planning is preserved from collapse under AVL.
  </details>

- **[RaDiVe: Robust 4D Radar Odometry with Distance-Bounded NDT and Velocity-Discrepancy Point Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28045)**  `arXiv:2607.28045`  
  _Sangwoo Jung, Dongjae Lee, Chiyun Noh, Ayoung Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in 4D radar enable robust perception in adverse weather; however, the inherent sparsity, noise, and limited positional precision of radar point clouds pose significant challenges for registration-based odometry. In this letter, we propose RaDiVe, a 4D radar odometry framework that improves the accuracy and robustness of radar point cloud registration. We introduce a distance-bounded Normal Distributions Transform, which improves optimization stability and computational efficiency by restricting the correspondence search to near-distance voxel pairs. To mitigate measurement ambiguity, we propose a velocity-discrepancy point uncertainty model that weights each input 4D radar point according to the discrepancy between its measured Doppler radial velocity and the radial velocity predicted from the estimated ego-velocity. We also incorporate Signed Distance Function-based surface point extraction via implicit neural mapping to construct a geometrically consistent, noise-filtered local submap. Evaluations across multiple public datasets demonstrate that RaDiVe outperforms existing 4D radar odometry baselines by 44.4% in translational and 21.3% in rotational Absolute Trajectory Error on average, while maintaining real-time performance.
  </details>

- **[Data Pyramid for Embodied Manipulation: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24744)**  `arXiv:2607.24744`  
  _Yifan Ye, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lv, Bohan Hou, Jun Cen, Lingdong Kong, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal foundation models learned to see and to speak by consuming the whole internet. Embodied agents admit no such shortcut, since they require data that couple observations with physical states and actions. These signals can be provided, to varying degrees, by multiple data sources. In this work, we organize the embodied data ecosystem as a "pyramid'' spanning five complementary sources: real-robot data, UMI-style data, egocentric and exocentric data, simulation data, and general vision-language data. We organize the pyramid around the tension between scalability and robot alignment, and further characterize each source in terms of data quality, diversity, reusability, and physical fidelity. We then analyze recent embodied foundation models through the lens of data recipes, examining how different sources are selected, aligned, and mixed during pretraining. For embodied brain models, vision-language-action models, and world-action models alike, we relate data composition to capabilities in perception, reasoning, planning, action generation, and world prediction. To facilitate community use, we additionally consolidate over 10,000 hours of trajectories from widely used robot datasets into a unified LeRobot format, with transparent frame-level quality annotations for filtering. We close by discussing six open challenges: building large-scale tactile datasets, collecting failure and recovery data, developing scalable data-collection pipelines, aligning actions across embodiments, leveraging egocentric data for dexterous manipulation, and designing principled data recipes for robot learning. We hope this work lays the foundation for the design of next-generation embodied systems.
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

However, effective specialization remains challenging, as it often requires substantial real-world data, and models adapted to one setting can still overfit to specific terrains or driving regimes. It then specializes the generalist model using limited real-world data and targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. On vegetation + dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to AnyCar fine-tuned on real data alone, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. With 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data and outperforms it when the terrain changes. Project Page :this https URL
  </details>

- **[Spatiotemporal and Multi-Robot Motion Planning on Graphs of Space-Time Convex Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00444)**  `arXiv:2607.00444`  
  _Jingtao Tang, Zining Mao, Lufan Yang, Hang Ma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Decoupled multi-robot motion planning avoids the high-dimensional joint configuration space but requires repeated single-robot planning among moving obstacles, where route choice and timing are coupled. We develop a framework based on graphs of space-time convex sets (ST-GCSs) for continuous spatiotemporal planning and multi-robot coordination. An ST-GCS represents collision-free space-time by convex sets, allowing the sequence of regions and the geometry and timing of piecewise-linear trajectories to be optimized jointly under velocity limits. To incorporate moving obstacles and previously planned robots, we develop Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD), which removes their swept occupancies while maintaining a convex decomposition for subsequent planning queries. Building on path-based GCS search, we develop a best-first solver tailored to the ST-GCS motion model, exploiting temporal reachability for dominance pruning and using admissible heuristics with separate or joint search-key evaluation. We integrate ST-GCS planning and ECD into prioritized multi-robot planning and introduce windowed coordination with dynamic window adjustment to limit reservation-induced graph growth. Experiments demonstrate improved scalability and competitive solution quality against optimization-based and sampling-based planners on challenging spatiotemporal and multi-robot problems. Large-scale simulations coordinate up to $100$ robots within a minute, while real-robot demonstrations showcase the practical applicability of the framework. Project homepage:this https URL.
  </details>

  _Phone Thiha Kyaw, Jonathan Kelly_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Informed sampling techniques accelerate sampling-based motion planners by focusing the search on promising regions of the state space, yet most existing methods rely on Euclidean heuristics that can become inadmissible under configuration-dependent Riemannian metrics. While scalar eigenvalue bounds restore admissibility by uniformly scaling the Euclidean distance, they discard the directional structure of the metric, producing overly conservative informed sets. We propose a matrix-valued admissible heuristic that exploits the Loewner order on symmetric positive definite matrices to compute the tightest constant lower bound on the metric tensor while retaining directional information discarded by scalar bounds. The Cholesky factorization of this constant bound maps the lower-bound informed set to a standard prolate hyperspheroid in Euclidean space, enabling direct, rejection-free sampling using existing algorithms. We then present an incremental algorithm for computing such a constant lower bound on the metric tensor from a sequence of pointwise evaluations. Experiments on manipulation tasks with a 6-DoF UR5, 7-DoF Franka, and 14-DoF PR2 under three distinct Riemannian metrics show that our heuristic produces consistently tighter informed sets than those produced by the Euclidean and scalar-eigenvalue heuristics, accelerating convergence across multiple state-of-the-art asymptotically optimal planners. Our implementation is available in the open-source geodex framework atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Direct Dynamic Retargeting for Humanoid Imitation Learning from Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23762)**  `arXiv:2605.23762`  
  _Constant Roux, Ludovic De Matteïs, Mathias Gatineau, Armand Jordana, Valentin Guillet, Nicolas Mansard, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Imitation Learning from monocular video demonstrations provides a scalable approach for teaching complex skills to humanoid robots. However, translating human motion to humanoids requires overcoming significant morphological mismatches. So far, dynamic retargeting methods obtain physically feasible references by tracking an intermediate geometric retargeting in simulation, usually through its joint angles. We show that this intermediate step biases the solution through two factors: the space in which the reference is tracked, joint angles rather than task-space keypoints, and the tracked reference itself, the keypoints of the geometric retargeting rather than those of the human demonstration. We propose Direct Dynamic Retargeting (DDR), which bypasses both: it tracks the human keypoints exclusively in task space with a sampling-based Model Predictive Control solver inside a physics simulator, without contact annotations. DDR is evaluated in simulation against joint-space dynamic retargeting under controlled conditions (identical solver, budget, and warm start), on three humanoids and on motions from monocular videos and motion capture. This advantage carries over to Reinforcement Learning imitation policies, which reproduce the human demonstration more faithfully than policies trained on joint-space dynamic references. These policies are deployed zero-shot on two physical humanoids of very different sizes, H1-2 and R1, including contact-rich motions.   </details>

- **[AoI-Aware Multi-Robot Sensing and Transport on Connected Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02107)**  `arXiv:2605.02107`  
  _John Tadrous_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A team of mobile robots monitors spatially distributed processes and delivers measurements to a base, where AoI is measured from sensing start, capturing both stochastic parallel sensing delays and hop-based propagation. At each non-base node, multiple robots may collaborate, yielding node-dependent geometric group sensing times, while other robots act as mobile conveyors that transport samples along unit-time edges. The paper first derives a per-node and network-wide AoI lower bound that decomposes into a sensing term, determined by mean group sensing times, and a propagation term, given by shortest-path distances. A shortest-path-tree conveyor architecture with an Euler-walk deployment is constructed and proven to attain the lower bound in a full-conveyor regime. Numerical simulations illustrate the impact of sensing allocation and conveyor deployment on AoI performance.
  </details>

- **[Agent-Centric Observation Adaptation for Robust Visual Control under Dynamic Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24661)**  `arXiv:2604.24661`  
  _Zhengru Fang, Yu Guo, Huanhuan Lou, Fei Liu, Yuang Zhang, Yihang Tao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual control maps visual streams to actions in reinforcement learning and vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Existing control benchmarks mainly test scene distractions, while generic restorers optimize whole-image fidelity. We introduce the Visual Degraded Control Suite (VDCS) to evaluate seven degradations under Markov switching. It also improves returns on DMC-GB and RoboSuite and retains 70% to 97% of clean-input mean return under six unseen perturbation families. We train ACO-MoE on robot demonstrations and deploy it with a 3B-parameter VLA policy on a Piper arm for cube placement in blue and white boxes and cup placement on a coaster. On the blue-box and cup tasks, motion blur and physical low light with added noise reduce success from 100% to at most 10%. ACO-MoE raises success to 75% to 95% over 20 trials per task and condition.
  </details>

- **[Trajectory Planning for Safe Dual Control with Active Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15507)**  `arXiv:2604.15507`  
  _Kaleb Ben Naveed, Manveer Singh, Devansh R. Agrawal, Dimitra Panagou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Planning safe trajectories under model uncertainty is a fundamental challenge. Robust planning ensures safety by considering worst-case realizations of the uncertainty with fixed uncertainty bounds, which leads to conservative behavior. Actively reducing uncertainty on-the-fly while planning for the system trajectories defines the dual control problem. Most approaches add a weighted exploration term to the mission cost, tuned to tradeoff the nominal objective and the uncertainty reduction, but without formal consideration of when exploration is beneficial to the mission. In addition, safety constraints are not in general considered in dual control approaches. In this paper we study a budget-constrained dual control problem, in which uncertainty is reduced while accounting for both safety constraints and a budget on the exploratory cost. To solve this problem we propose Dual-gatekeeper, a framework that integrates the nominal mission objective with active exploration under formal guarantees of safety and budget feasibility, so that exploratory actions are allowed only when safety and budget feasibility are then formally verified. We develop deterministic and probabilistic safety instantiations of the proposed approach, demonstrated through quadrotor navigation with uncertain aerodynamic parameters and autonomous racing with uncertain tire-road friction coefficients, respectively.
  </details>

- **[Delay-Aware Distributed Multi-Robot Motion Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18703)**  `arXiv:2511.18703`  
  _Ardalan Tajbakhsh, Augustinos Saravanos, James Zhu, Evangelos A. Theodorou, Lorenz T. Biegler, Aaron M. Johnson_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper examines why distributed optimization degrades when multi-robot systems coordinate under realistic communication delays. Using consensus ADMM as a representative framework for generating collision-free, dynamically feasible motion plans in both trajectory optimization and receding-horizon control settings, we show that delay degrades performance structurally: the consensus and dual updates weight stale and current information identically, so staleness enters the optimizer disguised as genuine disagreement and accumulates through the multipliers. Delay-agnostic adaptation (e.g. residual balancing) inherits this contamination and can perform worse than a fixed penalty. We introduce a Delay-Aware ADMM (DA-ADMM) variant that adapts penalty parameters to real-time delay statistics and re-derives the global consensus update as a delay-weighted average, down-weighting stale information in favor of recent updates. Simulations in 2D and 3D show that DA-ADMM improves robustness, success rate, and solution quality over fixed-parameter, residual-balancing, lower-bound, and fixed-constraint baselines. Degradation is therefore governed not by delay length or frequency, but by the optimizer's ability to reason over the age of the information it receives.
  </details>

- **[InFeR: Informed Failure Resilience in Learned Visual Navigation Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24680)**  `arXiv:2510.24680`  
  _Zishuo Wang, Joel Loo, David Hsu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While imitation learning (IL) has enabled successful visual navigation in many common environments, IL policies are prone to unpredictable failures under out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. This necessitates failure-resilient policies, which not only detect failures, but also recognise their sources and recover from them autonomously. We propose InFeR, a general framework for building IL policies with informed failure resilience without failure or recovery demonstrations. Given an IL policy's architecture and training dataset, InFeR retrains a new OOD-aware policy with a latent space structured for OOD failure detection, with a modified objective based on the Variational Information Bottleneck. It applies a visual explainability technique, Grad-CAM, to attribute failures to specific image regions and inform a heuristic policy for recovery. All these are achieved without requiring additional training data. Real-world experiments show that InFeR enables informed failure recovery across two different policy architectures, supporting long-range navigation in complex environments.
  </details>

- **[Human-like Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Driving using Knowledge Representation and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16498)**  `arXiv:2505.16498`  
  _Augusto Luis Ballardini, Miguel Ángel Sotelo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Achieving full automation in self-driving vehicles remains a challenge, especially in dynamic urban environments where navigation requires real-time adaptability. Existing systems struggle to handle navigation plans when faced with unpredictable changes in road layouts, spontaneous detours, or missing map data, due to their heavy reliance on predefined cartographic information. In this work, we explore the use of Large Language Models to generate Answer Set Programming rules by translating informal navigation instructions into structured, logic-based reasoning. ASP provides non-monotonic reasoning, allowing autonomous vehicles to adapt to evolving scenarios without relying on predefined maps. We present an experimental evaluation in which LLMs generate ASP constraints that encode real-world urban driving logic into a formal knowledge representation. By automating the translation of informal navigation instructions into logical rules, our method improves adaptability and explainability in autonomous navigation. Results show that LLM-driven ASP rule generation supports semantic-based decision-making, offering an explainable framework for dynamic navigation planning that aligns closely with how humans communicate navigational intent.
  </details>

- **[Nanorobot queue: Cooperative treatment of cancer based on team member communication and image processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.11236)**  `arXiv:2111.11236`  
  _Xinyu Zhou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although nanorobots have been used as clinical prescriptions for work such as gastroscopy, and even photoacoustic tomography technology has been proposed to control nanorobots to deliver drugs at designated delivery points in real time, and there are cases of eliminating "superbacteria" in blood through nanorobots, most technologies are immature, either with low efficiency or low accuracy, Either it can not be mass produced, so the most effective way to treat cancer diseases at this stage is through chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Patients are suffering and can not be cured. Therefore, this paper proposes an ideal model of a treatment method that can completely cure cancer, a cooperative treatment method based on nano robot queue through team member communication and computer vision image classification (target detection).
  </details>
